content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Predict the products of electrolysis of molten ionic compounds
Describe the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide
Explain why electrolysis is used to extract reactive metals

When a pure ionic compound is melted and electrolysed, predicting the products is straightforward - the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode. This process is essential for extracting reactive metals like aluminium.
The compound splits into its elements.
Silvery molten lead forms (sinks to bottom)
[DIAGRAM: Electrolysis cell showing molten lead bromide with carbon electrodes, lead collecting at bottom, bromine vapour at top]
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon
Electrolysis is the only method that works

[DIAGRAM: Cross-section of electrolysis cell for aluminium extraction showing: steel case, carbon lining (cathode), molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite, carbon anodes dipping into electrolyte, molten aluminium at bottom]
Cryolite lowers the melting point from 2050°C to about 950°C
Molten aluminium sinks to the bottom and is tapped off
Oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes
The anodes burn away and must be replaced regularly
Despite being the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, aluminium costs more than iron because of these extraction costs.
